one_liner: Tiny allocation-free C89 MessagePack reader/writer; smaller than msgpack-c but 13-30% slower on write in the only shootout.
what_it_does: Two files (cmp.c, cmp.h) implementing the MessagePack v5 spec, with *_v4 functions for peers that only speak spec v4. You fill a cmp_ctx_t with an opaque buf pointer plus reader, skipper and writer callbacks, then call typed writers (cmp_write_str, cmp_write_integer, cmp_write_array, ...) and typed or generic readers (cmp_read_str, cmp_read_object, cmp_skip_object_no_limit). There is no tree/DOM, no growable buffer and no allocation, so it is not a drop-in for msgpack-c's msgpack_packer/msgpack_sbuffer/unpacker API.
how_it_is_fast: It is not faster than msgpack-c; its design goal is minimal code and no buffering. Every value goes out as a one-byte type marker through one indirect ctx->write call and its length or payload through another, with byte swapping done by shift-based be16/be32/be64 helpers behind a runtime is_bigendian() test (compile-time if WORDS_BIGENDIAN is defined). That keeps the code to about 3.2 KB in the shootout's -O3 write build, but the extra callback per value is a plausible reason (our inference, not measured) why it trails msgpack C and MPack on encode throughput.
when_to_use: Firmware or other heap-less targets that need MessagePack in strict C89 with no malloc and no internal buffers (an ESP-IDF component CMakeLists.txt is shipped).
Streaming MessagePack straight to or from a file, socket or UART through your own read/write callbacks, without staging a whole message in RAM.
Schema-known messages decoded with typed readers (cmp_read_int, cmp_read_str) instead of building a tree.
Projects that want an MIT, two-file vendorable codec; c-toxcore vendors a TokTok fork as third_party/cmp.
when_not_to_use: Encode throughput matters: msgpack C 1.3.0 was 13-30% faster on every write row and MPack 0.8.1 about 3.4x faster (2.13 vs 7.33 us, small data, desktop) in the same shootout.
You need a DOM, random access or zero-copy reads: every value is memcpy'd through the read callback, and zero-copy reading (issue #29) has been open since 2016.
Size-optimized ARM builds: in the Raspberry Pi -Os build msgpack C's write path was smaller (1528 vs 2324 bytes) and still faster (67.35 vs 100.66 us).
You need stable versioning: no semver, the author says no version is guaranteed compatible with another, and only tagged releases are called stable.

integration.dependencies: none (stdbool.h, stddef.h, stdint.h, string.h); the test suite needs cmocka
integration.min_toolchain: C89 plus fixed-width integer types and bool (tests need C99)
integration.platforms: any; endianness detected at runtime or set with WORDS_BIGENDIAN; CMP_NO_FLOAT for FPU-less targets
integration.thread_safety: a context must not be shared between threads; one context per thread is fine (README 'thread aware')

gotchas: The README example and examples/example1.c and example2.c define the skipper as 'return fseek(...)'; fseek returns 0 on success, so the bool is false on every successful skip and true on failure. Since the 2025 commit 'Don't ignore errors reported by skip_bytes()' (PR #81, merged 2025-08-06), skips through that copied skipper fail; return fseek(...) == 0 instead.

cmp_read_str needs a buffer of at least str_size + 1 bytes (it NUL-terminates); when the string is too long it fails after consuming the marker and length but not the payload, leaving the stream mid-object, so the caller must skip str_size bytes itself.

Passing NULL read or write callbacks is allowed by cmp_init, but calling a read or write function then crashes (no check, per cmp.h); CMP_NO_FLOAT changes the ABI; cmp_skip_object_limit is deprecated after issue #45 (wrong on nested arrays), so use cmp_skip_object_flat or cmp_skip_object_no_limit.

The shootout ran CMP v14, which predates v16's fix for float bytes mangled on little-endian machines (issue #24, cmp_write_float/cmp_read_float) and v17's extra skip argument to cmp_init, so its harness no longer compiles against current CMP. The test writes only doubles and its output hashes matched msgpack-c, so the timed rows are not affected.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The catalogued siblings are C++ JSON or schema serializers (BitSerializer's MsgPack path, zpp::bits, Cap'n Proto), so pick CMP only when you need MessagePack from plain C with no allocation and tiny code; if C encode speed matters, MPack (ludocode/mpack, not yet catalogued) beat both msgpack-c and CMP in the same shootout.
verified_claims_summary: In ludocode/schemaless-benchmarks (2016, written by MPack's author; GCC 5.3.0 -O3 -flto, hash time subtracted), encoding random schemaless data into a growable buffer took CMP v14 7.33 us vs msgpack C 1.3.0 6.42 us (small) and 660.19 vs 544.24 us (large) on an AMD Phenom II X6 1090T, and 89.75 vs 69.21 us and 9206.05 vs 8142.64 us on a first-generation Raspberry Pi, with identical output hashes; CMP is 13-30% slower and the project publishes no numbers of its own. The harness code (cmp-write.c, buffer.h) treats both libraries alike: same object walk, a doubling buffer starting at 4 KB for CMP, one pass per run.
status_note: Low activity (last commit 2025-08-06, latest tagged release v20, which predates the 2024 cleanups and the 2025 skip-error fix) but MIT-licensed and two files, so easy to vendor; TokTok maintains a fork for c-toxcore.
